RAD kit activity guide

This RAD kit activity guide has been used on students ranging from the upper years of elementary school to Sec 5. While the activities are the same across grades, the depth of explanation and discussion will increase with the age of the students. A few points in the notes therefore are marked as only being for certain age groups.

For questions or comments, please contact Félix St-Amour (student in charge of activities) or Prof. H. Cynthia Chiang (group supervisor).

Acknowledgements

This document was created by Félix St-Amour. Carolina Cruz-Vinaccia, Alice Curtin, Mariah Zerough, Andrei Li, and Audrey Bernier helped structure the activity. The RAD kit is collaborative work between Félix St-Amour, Micheal Hétu, Olivia Locke, Maya Goss, and Eamon Egan. The outreach activity was created by the McGill Radio Lab under Prof. Cynthia Chiang.

Learning objectives

  • Understand properties of the dark age of the universe
    • Dark (no visible light)
    • Filled with neutral hydrogen
    • 21 cm light emitted by neutral hydrogen
  • Understand why antennas are used to probe the dark age
    • Radio light interacts with the antenna and gives us a signal
  • Understand why it is difficult to probe the dark age using antennas
    • Noise from radio sources on Earth
    • Ionosphere amplifies noise from Earth and dims 21 cm signal
    • Very dim signal from the early universe

Materials

  • 1 RAD kit per group of 4 students (provided)
  • 2 x AA for each RAD kit (provided)
  • Light prisms (provided)
  • 2 magnets per group of 4 students (provided)
  • Handheld radio with missing antenna (provided)

Procedure

  1. Introductions
    • Who we are:
      • Students at McGill who try to understand the universe and its history.
      • Physics teachers and communicators trying to share the good word of exploration and science.
    • Why are we here:
      • We want to discuss the history of the universe as we know it as well as some of its mysteries.
      • We want to study the dark age of the universe. This is a period that we know very little of and is really difficult to study. Let's figure out what it is and why it's so hard to study.
  2. Introduce the activity ideas
    • [BIG QUESTION OF THE INTRO] Why are we here? Why does the school and dirt it stands on exist?
    • We need to go back in time to see where everything started
      • Show all the way back to the primordial Earth. How did the Earth form?
      • Clouds of dust accumulate under gravity and form progressively larger clumps of dust until it resembles a planet.
      • Show the solar system when everything was just dust. Where does the dust come from?
      • Show that before the solar system, it was simply other stars and other dust. But where did the first stars and the first dust come from? We're going to do top down approach starting with the big bang.
    • Big Bang
      • What is the big bang? What does it look like?
      • Show a representation of the big bang. Probe: what is coming out of the big bang?
      • Go down: human → organs → cells → molecules → atoms → protons and electrons.
      • (For Sec ≥4) Photons ram electrons and eject them from atoms.
      • (For Sec <4) Electricity as a force has the same form as gravity. Take the example of earth and a comet. What are the possible orbits?
        • Low energy
          • Crash into the Earth
          • Example: We can think of an asteroid shooting down towards the Earth.
        • Medium energy
          • Orbit
          • Example: We can think of the moon on a stable orbit around the Earth (or the ISS).
        • High energy
          • Pass by, bend your path, leave
          • Example: We can think of an asteroid passing us and leaving forever.
      • (For Sec <4) The Big Bang had a lot of energy. Protons and electrons act like planets and asteroids; electrons fly by.
      • This is plasma, like the sun. Lots of light is being emitted. The universe would almost look white.
      • (For Sec ≥4) As the universe expands, photon density decreases (note that expansion also redshifts photos).
      • (For Sec ≥4) Expansion of the universe -> smaller photon density -> becomes dark.
      • Temperature of the universe at the end of Big Bang: 3000K. What is the temperature today?
        • Examples: absolute zero, sun surface, sun core, supernova.
        • Example: an astronaut has one side at +250 C and the other at -250 C.
        • The astronaut in empty space is in equilibrium with its surroundings (the universe).
        • Roughly -270 C which implies that it gradually cooled off. This means that the electrons and protons progressively lose energy.
      • (For Sec <4) Going back to the asteroid-earth model, we enter the circular orbit type.
      • Becomes less like the sun; no more light being produced.
      • Everything becomes dark!
    • We have reached the dark age of the universe. Nearly everything we observe from the universe comes in the form of light. To study the dark age, we need to refine our understanding of light.
    • The spectrum of light
      • Activity with the light prisms. Students get to scatter sunlight using the prisms and understand the white light is composed of multiple different colors that form a continuous spectrum.
      • Observation of a yellow flower and matching colors to the light spectrum.
      • Observation of a yellow flower using a bee's vision, identification of UV light past violet on the visible light spectrum.
      • Light has different wavelengths, each wavelength gives you a color.
      • Show that light is a wave:
        • Light travels at the speed of ... light.
        • If we look at the max of the wave, it crosses the border more frequently for the color blue than it does for the color red. Light crosses it more frequently? Frequency = color.
      • Examples of different "colors" on the EM spectrum.
        • Human in infrared: heat.
        • Human in UV: sunscreen is black.
        • Human in x-ray: bones (skips soft tissues).
      • Observation of the Crab nebula using visible light. Observation of the crab nebula under different frequencies of light.
    • Show a picture of the dark age of the universe using radio light. This is odd, why? (the universe looks to be a homogeneous color). Where does this color come from (21 cm)?
    • Earlier, we concluded that the universe, after the big bang, was made of electrons and protons. What type of matter does this lead to?
      • Neutral hydrogen has 1 proton and 1 electron. Entering quantum mechanics, both are either spin up or spin down.
      • Quantum configurations are like magnets: some configurations are more stable than others.
      • Give the magnet activity to determine the most stable configurations of the hydrogen atom.
      • Is a ball more stable on top of a hill or a valley?
      • Which ball has the most energy? Where does the energy go if we go from the highest energy to the lowest energy (both positions are rest, so energy is dissipated).
      • Are magnets more stable N-N or N-S?
      • H atom is most stable with antiparallel spins.This is like a N-S configuration.
      • When we go from unstable to stable, we release energy: 21 cm line! 10 My is the expected flip time.
    • We talked about how we would see the early universe if we were there, but how can we observe something that happened 13+ billion years ago?
      • What would happen if the sun exploded now? (when would we feel what happens?)
      • Photons travel for 8 minutes from the Sun to the Earth.
      • The Milky Way is 100,000 Ly across. What does it mean for our observations of distant stars?
      • In 2017, detection of gravitational wave GW170817. Comes from galaxy NGC 4993. This happened 144 My ago.
      • Light started traveling during the Jurassic. Traveled during the Cretaceous (T-Rex), saw the extinction of the dinos. Traveled during the Pleistocene (rodent-like mammals). Traveled when apes evolved. Traveled when the first humans evolved. Reached our detectors.
      • What do we see if we observe something 13.6 G.l.y. away (which is roughly the dark age)?
      • Why is it more red than earlier? (redshift)
      • As the universe expands, the wave of the light gets stretched to lower and lower frequencies (visible light shifts to the red). They lose energy!
    • Radio antenna to observe the dark age
      • ALBATROS from the McGill radio lab are used to observe the 21 cm line. Placed in Uapishka, QC, and MARS (McGill Arctic Research Station) Nunavut.
      • (For Sec < 4) How can we measure radio light?
        • What happens when you rub a balloon on your hair? What happens if you touch a door handle afterwards?
        • This is identical to accidentally shocking a cat when petting it.
        • Humans are made of atoms which have charges. These charges can move around.
        • What is electricity? Charges moving around.
        • Look at charged particles going through a wire.
        • Light has an electric component, meaning it can move around charged particles.
        • Charges are moved by the waves of light, exactly like a boat on waves.
        • Charged particles move right, stop, move left, and stop again.
        • We can measure electricity current/voltage; looks like the light wave!
        • Everything that has charged particles is an antenna!
      • (For Sec ≥ 4) Physical explanation
        • Show that light is an EM wave.
        • Show students model of the atom with protons and neutrons. Show equations of motion (with electric forces). Which one is the most affected by electric forces? Electrons or protons?
        • Assume protons don’t move. Look at the electric wave of light. What happens to the electrons? Guiding question: what is current?
        • Show a picture of a sine wave on an oscilloscope. This would be a pure signal from a light wave.
      • Everything is an antenna: Activity where a student uses their fingers to replace the antenna of a radio antenna.
      • Show the ALBATROS antenna used for research.
    • Big issues with observing 21 cm:
      • Very weak signal
        • If we look at a lightbulb, we can see photons coming out of it (roughly 1020 photons per second).
        • If we were to look at a hydrogen balloon at arm's length, would you be able to see the 21 cm photons coming out of it? Why?
        • Spin flip happens every 10 million years. Order of magnitude: how far away would a lightbulb have to be so that it's as bright as a balloon of hydrogen? (Answer: ~200km) Distance between Montreal and Quebec!
        • Why are we able to see the signal if it's so weak?
      • Other sources of radio noise
        • What is the frequency of a radio channel? Hint: how do we categorize radio channels? Radio: ~0.1GHz.
        • 21 cm redshifted to lower than 1.5GHz (0.15GHz); dangerously close to radio.
      • Ionosphere interference
        • What path does the light of a laser follow in air?
        • What can we see in this image of a pencil in a glass of water? Why is there a cut at the waterline? Does light follow a straight path?
        • Light bends when it passes from one medium to the next!
        • This is also what happened with the light prisms as well as lenses for vision.
        • Can light bend in such a way that it loops back around?
        • A mirage bends the light back towards us.
        • Do mirages affect all types of light in the same way? No, light prisms are an example.
        • The ionosphere (the highest part of our atmosphere) bends radio waves from earth back to us. Also bends back radio waves from outer space away from the earth.
  3. Introduce the experiment
    • RAD kits overview
      • Sound ↔ wave ↔ light
      • RAD has a microphone to hear the sounds around it
        • Frequency mode: maps the frequency of your voice (pitch) to a color.
        • Amplitude mode: maps how loud you are to the brightness of the light.
  4. Allow students to explore and test
    • Frequency noise
      • Use a pure tone generator at 190 Hz and put it next to the microphone. What do you observe?
      • Keep the true tone generator on. With you group, scream into the microphone. What do you observe?
      • Discuss with the group the relation between what they observed and radio noise on earth. How could they test radio waves bouncing back on the atmosphere?
      • What is the relation between light and sound waves? (Hint: color, amplitude)
    • Amplitude
      • The amplitude board is set to have parameters that show the white noise from the environment.
      • Before touching anything, what do they observe?
      • Allow them to move around and make noise. What do they observe? If not done already, how does it scale with distance? What do they think the relationship qualitatively is?
      • Does the noise overtake their voice at a distance? What does this mean for the signal?
      • How does this relate to the measurements of the ALBATROS antenna?
  5. Discuss
    • The discussion is part of the experiment itself.
  6. Wrap up
    • Dark age
      • Describe the dark age in 3 concepts (dark, hydrogen, cold, 21 cm, young universe, after the big bang,...).
    • Why is it hard to measure using antennas:
      • Scarcity of signal
      • Noise coming from the Earth
      • Noise amplified and signal reduced by ionosphere
